newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Emotional return for Bratunac refugees.
newsitem.headline: Emotional return for Bratunac refugees.

text.p: Twenty one Moslems driven from their homes by Serbs in the eastern Bosnian town of Bratunac when war erupted in 1992 returned for the first time on Saturday to vote.
A bus guarded by U.N. police and American NATO troops drove them to the village of Djugum, just outside Bratunac, where they cast their ballots without incident.
It was an emotional return to an area which generated intense ethnic hatred during the war.

Hostile Bratunac Serbs regularly blocked U.N. food convoys to the starving nearby Moslem enclave of Srebrenica during a siege by the Bosnian Serb Army that ended in a massacre of Moslem prisoners when it fell in 1995.
Revenge guerrilla raids by Moslem fighters from Srebrenica inflicted heavy casualties on surrounding Serb villages.
Most of the Moslem voters on Saturday were elderly or middle aged, apart from a man of 21.

"I came to see my Bratunac. I just want them to let us come back. I want to live where my grandfather died," said 64-year-old Ibrahim Hodzic. "I am voting today because I wanted to see my town up close. I hope it won't be the last time."

He found it disturbing to drive past Moslem homes torched during Serb ethnic cleansing early in the war. "It's very hard to look at these homes that were burnt down. My two sons who were in Srebrenica are still missing," he said, breaking into tears.
Serb representatives running the polling stations treated the Moslems politely, recognising former neighbours among them.
The Moslems said they were not afraid of venturing into Serb-controlled territory after 3/-1/2 years of a Serb campaign of explusion and terror directed against them in eastern Bosnia.
"I have no fear," said Mira Zebic, 41. "I see all my husbands' former colleagues here. They all know me. I'm not scared...it's important to vote in the place you come from."
Zebic said she was ready to live with Serbs again and to bury the memories of bloodshed. She added: "We have to search for peace among people, in our souls and in our children."
U.N. police expected more buses to arrive from the Moslem-Croat federation some of them carrying refugees from Srebrenica.
They were voting on the first floor of a partially destroyed house, formerly inhabited by Moslems.

A Serb family, refugees from Sarajevo, have moved into the second floor. Serbs sat outside in the sun playing cards as the Moslems voted and tried to pretend that nothing extaordinary was taking place.
"People are exercising their free will to chose their candidates. It doesn't bother me. They should live as well." said Zaga Kenjac, 37.
But she ruled out living with Moslems again."That's out of the question. I left two houses behind (in Sarajevo)."
Her husband Rajko Kenjac said the Bosnian Serbs would not be threatened by Moslems voting. "They are a minority here, they don't stand a chance."
